name: pulse-compare-threaded-vs-event-loop
notes:
Flip 'server profile' live: threaded (bounded workers, real admission control) vs event-loop (unlimited workers, node.js-style) against the same 5x pulse (700rps -> 3500rps over 5s, held 15s, back down over 5s -- shorter than the 30s boot time, so no capacity added mid-pulse can help). Per-request CPU time and I/O wait are exponential (shifted-exp, near-zero floor + an exponential tail: cpuTimeMs mean ~16ms, ioWaitMs mean ~51ms) for real service-time variance. metricCpuTarget is 0.7 -- deliberately high. The point of this preset is a well-behaved unit driven HOT, not one running with generous headroom: threaded's admission control is what makes 70% sustainable at all, not a low target. Both variants start at the same 4 instances (`initialInstances`), sized for the 700rps base load at that target.

Threaded's worker count is tuned to 25 (queueSlots: 0 -- reject immediately once busy, no extra waiting room) to land exactly on the edge: fewer workers (e.g. 15) sheds even at steady state (~5% baseline errors, target overshoots into rejection before any pulse); more (40+) admits everything but lets p95 climb well past baseline during the burst (workers=60 -> peak p95 ~354ms). 25 is the sweet spot -- 0% errors at steady state (69% measured utilization, matching the 70% target almost exactly) and only a small, bounded rise during the pulse itself.

Measured (seeds 1-5): threaded holds steady-state errors at 0% and, even at 70% target utilization, keeps p95 to ~208-210ms during the pulse (baseline is ~165-180ms -- a small, real but modest rise) for ~5.4-5.6% rejected, essentially all inside the burst window. It's a well-behaved unit driven hard, not an idle one coasting through the pulse on spare capacity.

Event-loop -- same pulse, same 700rps/70%-target base, only workers unbounded -- on equal hardware: Node processes are single-core, so the slide overrides cores=1 with initialInstances=16 (maxInstances=80) to match the threaded fleet's 4 instances x 4 cores = 16 cores. Pre-pulse p95 is ~175-210ms in both. Clients (both variants) give up after clientTimeoutSec=10 -- a realistic LB/proxy timeout; threaded never gets near it. Memory is NOT modelled; the only hard concurrency limit is the internal 5000-slot cap per instance, which this pulse doesn't reach on 16 instances. Event-loop never rejects, so it builds a queue; waits climb past 10s, ~100k requests time out and show up as ~11% errors (measured: errors 11.3%, OK-request p95 capped near 10s instead of ~50s without the timeout, same ~3 min drain because abandoned requests still burn CPU server-side). Threaded instead rejects ~5.3% inside the burst, instantly, and p95 stays ~208ms. Twice the error rate, and a very different failure: a fast 'no' in milliseconds vs a slow 'no' after 10s of waiting, with the doomed work still executed. Same load, same variance, same hardware, same aggressive target -- the only variable is whether the unit can say no, and to what. A well-behaved unit can be run hot; a unit with no admission control cannot, no matter what target you set it to.
